_note: Independent worked examples for the standard atmosphere: pressure altitude from an altimeter setting, density altitude and standard temperature, each from the FAA's own handbook or testing supplement (fetched from faa.gov on 2026-11-21), never from the code. Each case names the engine rule asked by name (engine/facade/tests/reference.rs), the expected figure, the tolerance the source's rounding implies, the source's page and figure, and where the source's method differs from the engine's, what it is. Checks: value within tolerance of the answer at path ("" the whole answer), at_least, equals.

cases.name: Sample Problem 1: 5,883 ft and 30.10 inHg is a pressure altitude of 5,718 ft
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 11, p. 11-20, Sample Problem 1: "Find 30.10 under the altimeter heading ... It reads “–165.” Therefore, it is necessary to subtract 165 from the airport elevation giving a pressure altitude of 5,718 feet."
cases.method: The table's factor in whole feet: within 2 ft.

cases.name: Sample Problem 1: 5,718 ft pressure altitude at 70 °F is a density altitude of about 7,700 ft
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 11, p. 11-20, Sample Problem 1 (Figure 11-22): "From 70°, draw a line up to the 5,718 feet pressure altitude line ... The approximate density altitude in thousands of feet is 7,700 feet." 70 °F is 21.11 °C.
cases.method: The handbook reads its chart to the nearest hundred feet; the engine works density altitude from the standard atmosphere's density (about 7,709 ft), more exact than the chart, so within 100 ft.

cases.name: A pressure altitude of 5,000 ft at 20 °C above standard is a density altitude above 7,000 ft
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, 2023), ch. 11, p. 11-4: "the altimeter may indicate a pressure altitude of 5,000 feet ... if the temperature is 20 °C above standard ... it may be found that the density level is above 7,000 feet". Standard at 5,000 ft is 5.1 °C (Figure 11-2), so 25.1 °C.
cases.method: The handbook gives a bound, not a figure: the engine's (about 7,270 ft) must be above it.
